title: How did Latin turn into Portuguese?
hook: Nobody woke up one day speaking Portuguese: the language changed bit by bit, over centuries.
summary: The spoken Latin the Romans brought to the Iberian Peninsula slowly changed; in the northwest it became Galician-Portuguese, the root of Portuguese.
cardText: Slowly. The spoken Latin the Romans brought to the Iberian Peninsula changed over centuries. In the peninsula’s northwest it became Galician-Portuguese, the root of today’s Portuguese.

cardBlocks.text: Roman armies reached the Iberian Peninsula during the war against Carthage that began in 218 BC, and when it ended the region passed to Rome. They brought Latin with them, but not the Latin of books: the Latin spoken by ordinary people, soldiers and farmers. Over the centuries, that everyday Latin turned into Portuguese.

By around AD 600, it is thought, Vulgar Latin had given way to new languages, the Romance languages. In the peninsula’s northwest, Galician-Portuguese emerged, and words kept shifting: manu became mão (hand), clamare became chamar (to call). That is why Portuguese is a Romance language, a sister of Spanish, Italian and French.
Portuguese is the Romans’ spoken Latin, reshaped over centuries in the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Romans didn’t speak a single Latin. There was the sermo urbanus of the educated and the sermo plebeius of ordinary people: farmers, soldiers and foreigners. Portuguese carries on that people’s Latin in all its varieties.
The language that came down from the north

After the Muslim conquest, the south of the peninsula spoke Mozarabic, a much-changed Latin full of Arabic influence. The Portuguese linguist Fernando Venâncio argues that during the Christian Reconquista it was the Galician of the northwest that moved south with the court, the soldiers and the administration, and replaced those dialects.

One clue is in the sounds. In the northwest, l and n between vowels dropped out, which didn’t happen in Spanish: Latin colore gave Spanish color but Portuguese cor. The same goes for dolor and dor, corona and coroa.
When the language got its name

Continuous texts in the language appear around 1192. But the name “Portuguese” is first found in writing, as far as anyone knows, in 1430, when Prince Pedro, translating a book by Cicero, wrote that he had read chapters of it aloud “em portugues” to others.

Latium was the ancient region of central Italy whose history is bound up with Rome’s. The Brazilian poet Olavo Bilac, a founder of the Brazilian Academy of Letters, opened his sonnet “Língua Portuguesa”, published in the book Tarde (1919), with the line “Última flor do Lácio, inculta e bela” (“last flower of Latium, uncultivated and beautiful”). The image is usually read as Portuguese being the last of the languages born from Vulgar Latin.

claims.text: By around AD 600, it is thought, Vulgar Latin was no longer spoken anywhere in the former empire; new languages, the Romance languages, had taken its place.

claims.text: According to Fernando Venâncio, during the Reconquista the Galician of the north spread south and replaced the Mozarabic dialects, a much-changed Latin influenced by Arabic.

support.excerpt: Venâncio propõe que foi o galego que se espalhou para o Sul da futura região portuguesa durante a Reconquista cristã (e não um suposto “português primitivo”), substituindo os falares moçárabes, que predominavam desde a ocupação muçulmana.

No Sul, falava-se ainda latim hispânico já muito mudado e com muitas influências árabes − a língua a que chamamos hoje moçárabe. A língua do Norte era a língua da corte e dos soldados, da administração.
